question: A section with 4 % camber is at zero geometric angle of attack. Its lift and moment about the aerodynamic centre are:

options.text: Negative lift and a nose-up moment
Positive lift and a nose-down moment

explanation: Camber places the zero-lift angle below zero (α₀ < 0), so at α = 0 the section operates at α − α₀ > 0: cl > 0. Camber also produces a negative (nose-down) C_M,ac, constant with α.

question: A section with zero-lift angle α₀ = −3° is set at a geometric angle of attack of +2°. The absolute angle of attack is:
explanation: Absolute angle of attack is measured from the zero-lift line: α_abs = α − α₀ = 2 − (−3) = 5°. Lift is proportional to α_abs below the stall: cl = a₀·α_abs.

question: Within a family of similar sections, leading-edge radius scales with (t/c)². The leading-edge radius of the 15 % thick section compared with the 9 % section is:
explanation: r_LE ∝ (t/c)²: (15/9)² = 1.667² = 2.78. The larger radius lowers the suction peak at high α and delays leading-edge separation.

question: Moving the point of maximum thickness aft (e.g. from 30 % to 45 % chord) at low angle of attack has the effect that:

options.text: The minimum-pressure point moves aft, extending the favourable gradient and the laminar run
Skin friction increases, because the turbulent region lengthens
The minimum-pressure point moves forward, shortening the laminar run

explanation: Velocity peaks near maximum thickness at low α. Upstream of the minimum-pressure point the pressure gradient is favourable (dp/dx < 0), which stabilises laminar flow. An aft peak keeps the boundary layer laminar farther back and reduces skin friction within a limited cl range.

question: A symmetric section with lift-curve slope 0.11 per degree is at α = −4°. cl and C_M,ac are:
explanation: Symmetric section: α₀ = 0, cl = 0.11 × (−4) = −0.44. With no camber, C_M,ac = 0 and the centre of pressure stays at the aerodynamic centre at all α below the stall.

question: To produce the same cl, a cambered section compared with a symmetric section of the same thickness requires:

options.text: A lower chord-line angle of attack
A higher chord-line angle of attack
A negative angle of attack in every case

explanation: Both have the same slope a₀; camber displaces the curve by α₀ < 0. For equal cl, α_cambered = α_symmetric + α₀, which is lower.

question: As the angle of attack increases below the stall, the front stagnation point:

options.text: Moves up onto the upper surface
Moves toward the trailing edge on the upper surface
Moves down and aft on the lower surface
Remains fixed at the leading edge

explanation: Higher α increases circulation. Flow reaching the upper surface must travel round the leading edge from a stagnation point that migrates to the lower surface, aft of the leading edge. This steepens the suction peak just behind the leading edge.

question: As the upper-surface suction peak rises with increasing α, the pressure recovery downstream of it:

options.text: Is unaffected, since it depends only on the trailing-edge angle
Steepens, increasing the adverse pressure gradient on the boundary layer

explanation: The flow must return from the peak suction to near free-stream pressure at the trailing edge. A deeper peak over the same chord requires a larger pressure rise: dp/dx grows. The boundary layer eventually cannot negotiate it, and separation marks the stall.

question: At a moderate positive angle of attack, the larger share of section lift comes from:

options.text: The pressure difference at the trailing edge

explanation: |Cp| on the upper surface reaches −1 to −3 near the leading edge, whereas lower-surface Cp stays between 0 and about +1 except at the stagnation point. Typically about two-thirds or more of cl comes from the upper surface.

question: The chordwise-averaged pressure-coefficient difference between the lower and upper surfaces is 0.8. The section lift coefficient is:
explanation: cl = ∫₀¹ (Cp,lower − Cp,upper) d(x/c) = mean ΔCp = 0.8. Lift equals the area enclosed by the two Cp curves.

question: A symmetric section at zero angle of attack has:

options.text: Overpressure on both surfaces and zero lift
Suction on the upper surface only
Zero pressure change on both surfaces
Equal suction on both surfaces and zero net lift

explanation: Thickness accelerates the flow over both surfaces, producing identical negative Cp distributions. The pressure difference, and hence lift, is zero. Thickness alone does not lift; incidence and camber do.

question: A chordwise loading ΔCp falls linearly from a maximum at the leading edge to zero at the trailing edge. The centre of pressure is at:
explanation: The centre of pressure is the centroid of the load distribution. A triangle with its apex at the leading edge has its centroid at one third of the base from that edge: x_cp = c/3.

question: Thin-aerofoil theory gives a lift-curve slope of 2π per radian. At α_abs = 5°, cl is:
explanation: cl = 2π·α with α in radians: 5° = 0.0873 rad → cl = 6.283 × 0.0873 = 0.548. 2π per radian = 0.1097 per degree. 31.4 omits the conversion.

question: A section has α₀ = −2° and a₀ = 0.11 per degree. At α = +4°, cl is:
explanation: cl = a₀(α − α₀) = 0.11 × (4 + 2) = 0.66. 0.44 ignores α₀; 0.22 subtracts it with the wrong sign.

question: A section has α₀ = −1° and a₀ = 0.11 per degree. The angle of attack for cl = 1.0 is closest to:
explanation: α = cl/a₀ + α₀ = 9.1 − 1 = 8.1°. 9° ignores α₀; 10° adds it with the wrong sign.

question: Adding camber to a section of the same thickness changes the cl–α curve as follows:

options.text: It shifts right and becomes steeper
It shifts left and clmax decreases
It shifts left (α₀ more negative), keeps the same slope, and raises clmax
Its slope increases in proportion to camber

explanation: Thin-aerofoil theory: slope 2π is independent of camber; camber only sets α₀. The more favourable leading-edge pressure distribution at high cl typically raises clmax, although the stall α is similar or slightly lower.

question: For an elliptically loaded wing of aspect ratio 12, the ratio of the three-dimensional lift-curve slope to the section slope (2π) is closest to:
explanation: a = 2π·A/(A + 2) → a/a₀ = A/(A + 2) = 12/14 = 0.857. Downwash reduces effective incidence, so a finite wing always has a lower lift-curve slope than its section.

question: A section with cl = 0.8 operates at q = 3,000 Pa and chord 2 m. The lift per unit span is:
Beyond the stall angle, a conventional section's cl, cd and C_M,ac respond as follows:

options.text: cl is constant and cd rises linearly
cl falls, cd falls, and the moment becomes nose-up
cl falls, cd rises steeply, and the pitching moment becomes more nose-down
cl continues to rise at a reduced slope, and cd is constant

explanation: Upper-surface separation collapses the suction peak and forms a wide wake. Lift is lost, pressure drag rises sharply, and the remaining load distribution moves toward mid-chord, increasing the nose-down moment about the quarter chord.

question: The lift-curve slope of an elliptically loaded wing of aspect ratio 8 is closest to:
explanation: a = a₀/(1 + a₀/(πA)) = 6.283/(1 + 6.283/25.13) = 6.283/1.25 = 5.03 per rad = 0.0877 per degree. 0.073 corresponds to A = 4; 0.110 to the section value.

question: Elliptically loaded wings of aspect ratio 8 and 4 must each produce CL = 0.6. The angles of attack above zero lift are:
An elliptically loaded wing of aspect ratio 8 operates at CL = 0.5. The induced angle of attack is:
explanation: α_i = CL/(πA) = 0.5/25.13 = 0.0199 rad = 1.14°. 0.020° is the radian value misread as degrees.

question: Compared with a high-aspect-ratio wing using the same section, a low-aspect-ratio wing has:

options.text: A shallower lift-curve slope and a higher stalling angle
A steeper lift-curve slope and a lower stalling angle
The same slope and stalling angle
A steeper slope and a higher CLmax

explanation: Lower A → larger α_i per unit CL, so a = a₀/(1 + a₀/(πA)) is smaller. The wing reaches the section's stalling α_eff only at a higher geometric α. CLmax is similar or slightly lower.

question: Sweeping a wing by 35° at constant span loading reduces its lift-curve slope to approximately the unswept value times:
explanation: Simple sweep theory: only the velocity component normal to the leading edge, V·cosΛ, generates the pressure distribution, so the slope based on free-stream q scales with cosΛ = cos35° = 0.819. 0.57 is sin35°; 0.67 is cos²35°.

question: A wing with span efficiency factor e = 0.8 is compared with an elliptically loaded wing (e = 1) of the same aspect ratio at the same CL. Its induced angle is larger by the factor:
explanation: α_i = CL/(πeA) ∝ 1/e = 1/0.8 = 1.25. Induced drag coefficient CL²/(πeA) is higher by the same factor.

question: At equal CL and span efficiency, the induced-drag coefficient of a wing with aspect ratio 10 compared with one of aspect ratio 5 is:
explanation: CD,i = CL²/(πeA) ∝ 1/A → 5/10 = 0.5. For equal area, doubling A means span ×√2.

question: Far behind an elliptically loaded wing, the downwash angle compared with the induced angle at the wing is:

options.text: Zero, because the trailing vortices have dissipated
Twice as large; a tailplane lies in a region between the two values

explanation: The trailing vortex sheet is semi-infinite at the wing (half-contribution) and effectively infinite far downstream, so ε∞ = 2α_i. The downwash at the tailplane lies between these limits and varies with CL, reducing tail angle of attack.

subtopic: Aerodynamic centre and centre of pressure
question: A section has C_M,ac = −0.06 with the aerodynamic centre at 0.25c, and operates at cl = 0.3. The centre of pressure is at:
explanation: x_cp = x_ac − C_M,ac/cl = 0.25 + 0.06/0.3 = 0.45c. With a nose-down C_M,ac the centre of pressure lies aft of the aerodynamic centre.

subtopic: Aerodynamic centre and centre of pressure
question: For the section with C_M,ac = −0.06 (x_ac = 0.25c), cl increases from 0.3 to 1.2. The centre of pressure:
explanation: At cl = 0.3: 0.25 + 0.2 = 0.45c. At cl = 1.2: 0.25 + 0.05 = 0.30c. Forward movement of 0.15c; x_cp approaches x_ac asymptotically as cl rises.

subtopic: Aerodynamic centre and centre of pressure
question: As cl of a positively cambered section tends to zero, the centre of pressure:

options.text: Moves toward infinity aft; the section carries a pure couple

explanation: x_cp = x_ac − C_M,ac/cl. With C_M,ac < 0 and cl → 0⁺, the term grows without bound. At zero lift the upper and lower loads are equal and opposite but separated: a pure nose-down couple with no defined point of action.

subtopic: Aerodynamic centre and centre of pressure
question: A section has C_M,ac = −0.05 at x_ac = 0.25c and cl = 0.8. The moment coefficient about the leading edge is:
explanation: C_M,LE = C_M,ac − cl·x_ac = −0.05 − 0.8 × 0.25 = −0.25. Lift acting aft of the leading edge adds a nose-down contribution.

subtopic: Aerodynamic centre and centre of pressure
question: For the same section (C_M,ac = −0.05, x_ac = 0.25c, cl = 0.8), the moment coefficient about the mid-chord point is:
explanation: C_M,x = C_M,ac + cl(x − x_ac) = −0.05 + 0.8 × 0.25 = +0.15. Lift acting ahead of the reference point produces a nose-up contribution.

subtopic: Aerodynamic centre and centre of pressure
question: Moments measured about 0.20c are C_M = −0.06 at cl = 0.2 and C_M = −0.10 at cl = 1.0. The aerodynamic centre and C_M,ac are:

subtopic: Aerodynamic centre and centre of pressure
question: For a symmetric section below the stall, the centre of pressure:

options.text: Remains at the aerodynamic centre at all angles of attack

explanation: C_M,ac = 0 → x_cp = x_ac − 0/cl = x_ac, independent of α. Hence symmetric sections are used where zero centre-of-pressure travel is required.

subtopic: Aerodynamic centre and centre of pressure
question: In supersonic flow, the aerodynamic centre of a thin section lies near:
explanation: Linearised supersonic theory gives a uniform ΔCp over a flat plate at incidence, so the load centroid is at mid-chord. The aft movement from 25 % through the transonic range increases longitudinal stability and trim demand.

subtopic: Aerodynamic centre and centre of pressure
question: A section of 2 m chord has L′ = 5,000 N/m and a moment about its aerodynamic centre of −1,000 N·m per metre. The centre of pressure is located:
explanation: Distance = −M_ac/L′ = 1,000/5,000 = 0.2 m = 0.10c aft. A negative (nose-down) moment places the centre of pressure aft of the aerodynamic centre.

subtopic: Aerodynamic centre and centre of pressure
question: The aerodynamic centre is the preferred reference for section moments because:

options.text: It coincides with the centre of gravity
The moment about it is always zero
The moment about it is independent of angle of attack below the stall
Lift acts through it at all angles of attack

explanation: Differentiating C_M,x = C_M,ac + cl(x − x_ac) with respect to cl gives zero only at x = x_ac. Aerodynamics about the aerodynamic centre reduce to lift plus a constant couple, which simplifies stability analysis; the centre of pressure moves, the aerodynamic centre does not.

question: A reflexed trailing edge (upturned camber line aft) produces:

options.text: A strongly nose-down C_M,ac and higher clmax
C_M,ac near zero or positive, at the cost of lower clmax
A positive zero-lift angle and higher clmax

explanation: Reflex creates a local down-load at the trailing edge, cancelling the nose-down moment of forward camber. Tailless aircraft use it for self-trim; the smaller effective camber lowers clmax.

question: Increasing camber at constant thickness changes α₀, C_M,ac and clmax as follows:

options.text: α₀ more negative, C_M,ac unchanged, clmax lower
α₀ more positive, C_M,ac more positive, clmax higher
α₀ more negative, C_M,ac more negative, clmax higher
α₀ unchanged, C_M,ac more negative, clmax lower

explanation: Thin-aerofoil theory: both α₀ and C_M,ac are linear in camber and negative for positive camber. clmax rises until the steeper aft pressure recovery triggers trailing-edge separation.

question: A section with negative camber (camber line below the chord) has:

options.text: A positive zero-lift angle and zero moment
A zero-lift angle of zero and a nose-down C_M,ac
A positive zero-lift angle and a nose-up C_M,ac
A negative zero-lift angle and a nose-down C_M,ac

explanation: Reversing the camber reverses the signs: α₀ > 0 and C_M,ac > 0. Such a section produces its best cl in the negative direction.

question: Horizontal tail surfaces commonly use symmetric or negatively cambered sections because:

options.text: They must generate lift in both directions and often carry a trim download
Positive camber would increase their Reynolds number
Symmetric sections have a higher lift-curve slope
Tailplanes operate at zero lift at all times

explanation: In a conventional trimmed configuration the tail load is usually downward and changes sign with CG position, configuration and manoeuvre. A symmetric section gives equal capability either way; negative camber optimises for download.

subtopic: Aerodynamic centre and centre of pressure
question: EAS is doubled at constant C_M,ac. The pitching moment about the aerodynamic centre changes by the factor:
explanation: M_ac = C_M,ac·q·S·c with q ∝ V_E² → ×4. At high speed the nose-down couple grows with q even though lift is held constant by lower α; the elevator/stabiliser trim load grows correspondingly.

question: Section thickness increases from 6 % to 12 % of chord. clmax, profile drag and critical Mach number change as follows:

options.text: clmax falls, profile drag falls, critical Mach number rises
clmax rises, profile drag falls, critical Mach number rises
clmax rises, profile drag rises, critical Mach number falls

explanation: A thicker section has a larger leading-edge radius, delaying leading-edge separation (higher clmax). Higher super-velocities raise pressure drag and bring local M = 1 at a lower free-stream Mach number.

question: For conventional low-speed sections, clmax as a function of thickness ratio:

options.text: Peaks near 12–15 % and falls for thicker or thinner sections

explanation: Thin sections stall by leading-edge separation (small r_LE); very thick sections stall by trailing-edge separation from steep aft recovery. The maximum lies between these regimes.

question: Reducing the leading-edge radius at constant thickness ratio results in:

options.text: A flatter suction peak and a gentler stall
A sharper suction peak and earlier, more abrupt leading-edge separation
Higher clmax and a more gradual stall

explanation: Flow turning round a small radius requires high local velocity: steep suction peak followed by a severe adverse gradient. Separation starts at the leading edge at lower α and spreads rapidly — a sudden lift loss.

question: The profile-drag component that grows with thickness ratio at constant Reynolds number is predominantly:

options.text: Wave drag at low subsonic speed

explanation: Profile drag = skin friction + form drag. Thickness increases super-velocities and the aft pressure recovery, thickening the boundary layer and leaving an unrecovered pressure deficit at the trailing edge.

question: Sections with maximum thickness far aft (laminar-flow sections) typically show:

options.text: Lower drag at all cl and a gentle stall
A low-drag bucket in a narrow cl range and a sharp stall sensitive to contamination

explanation: Favourable gradient to ~40–60 % chord sustains laminar flow only near the design cl. Outside the bucket, or with roughness or contamination, transition moves forward and cd rises abruptly. The small leading-edge radius gives an abrupt stall.

question: A straight-tapered wing has span 30 m, root chord 5 m and taper ratio 0.4. Wing area and aspect ratio are:
explanation: c_t = λ·c_r = 2 m. S = b(c_r + c_t)/2 = 30 × 3.5 = 105 m². A = b²/S = 900/105 = 8.57. 150 m² treats the wing as rectangular.

question: For the wing with root chord 5 m and taper ratio 0.4, the mean aerodynamic chord is closest to:
explanation: MAC = (2/3)·c_r·(1 + λ + λ²)/(1 + λ) = (2/3) × 5 × 1.56/1.4 = 3.71 m. 3.50 m is the mean geometric chord S/b. MAC is weighted by chord², so it exceeds the geometric mean for a tapered wing.

question: On an untwisted rectangular wing, the stall begins:
explanation: Downwash is strongest near the tips of a rectangular wing, so local α_eff and cl are highest at the root. The root reaches clmax first; separation at the root gives buffet on the tail and preserves aileron effectiveness.

question: A strongly tapered wing (taper ratio about 0.2) without twist has:

options.text: A root-stall tendency, because the root chord is largest
No tendency, since taper affects only drag
A tip-stall tendency, because local cl peaks near the tips

explanation: Decreasing chord with nearly elliptical load requires higher local cl outboard: cl ∝ loading/chord. Tip sections also operate at lower Re, reducing local clmax. Stall begins outboard, with roll-off and loss of aileron effectiveness.

question: A wing with an elliptical chord distribution and no twist:

options.text: Has uniform local cl and stalls across the whole span at once

explanation: Elliptical loading gives uniform downwash, so every section operates at the same α_eff and cl. All sections reach clmax together: minimum induced drag, but no warning and no roll control margin at stall.

question: Root sections stall at 15° local incidence and the wing has 2.5° of linear geometric washout. When the root reaches 15°, the tip incidence is:

options.text: 10°, since washout doubles toward the tip
15°, so the whole wing stalls together

explanation: Washout reduces incidence toward the tip: α_tip = α_root − 2.5° = 12.5°, below the section stall angle. The tip retains 2.5° margin, maintaining aileron authority.

question: Aerodynamic washout is produced by:

options.text: Increasing geometric incidence toward the tip
Tip sections with less camber (zero-lift angle closer to zero) than root sections

explanation: A less-cambered tip produces less lift at the same geometric incidence (smaller α − α₀), which has the same effect as a geometric twist of α₀,root − α₀,tip.

question: A swept-back wing tends to stall first at the tips because:

options.text: Sweep reduces local cl at the tips
Spanwise flow thickens the outboard boundary layer and the inboard wing induces upwash on the tips
Sweep moves the aerodynamic centre forward
Tips operate at higher Reynolds number

explanation: The spanwise pressure gradient drives low-energy boundary-layer air outboard, thickening it at the tips. The swept geometry loads the outer panels. Tip stall moves the centre of lift forward and produces pitch-up.

question: An elliptically loaded wing has semi-span 15 m. The spanwise centre of lift on each semi-span lies at:
explanation: The centroid of a quarter ellipse is at 4s/(3π) = 0.424s = 0.424 × 15 = 6.37 m. This spanwise position sets the root bending moment per unit lift.

question: A wing has A = 6, e = 0.9, CL = 0.8 and geometric angle of attack 8°. The effective angle of attack is:
explanation: α_i = CL/(πeA) = 0.8/16.96 = 0.0472 rad = 2.70°. α_eff = 8 − 2.7 = 5.3°. 7.95° subtracts the radian value; 2.7° is α_i itself.

question: For the wing with A = 6, e = 0.9 and CL = 0.8, the induced-drag coefficient is:
explanation: CD,i = CL²/(πeA) = 0.64/16.96 = 0.0377. 0.034 omits e; 0.047 uses CL instead of CL².

question: At constant weight and altitude, the aircraft doubles its airspeed in level flight. The induced angle of attack changes by the factor:
explanation: CL = W/(qS) ∝ 1/V² → ×¼. α_i = CL/(πeA) ∝ CL → ×¼. Induced drag D_i = q·S·CD,i ∝ V²·V⁻⁴ ∝ 1/V² also falls to ¼.

question: Within about one span of the ground, a wing at constant angle of attack experiences:

options.text: Reduced downwash and induced drag, and an increased lift-curve slope
Reduced lift and increased induced drag
No change in lift or drag

explanation: The ground constrains the vertical velocity of the trailing vortex system (image vortices), reducing downwash. α_eff rises toward α, raising CL for a given α and lowering CD,i. The reduced downwash at the tail also reduces the tail download, producing nose-down pitch.

question: Reynolds number increases tenfold at the same Mach number. Section clmax and minimum cd change as follows:

options.text: clmax rises and minimum cd falls
clmax rises and minimum cd rises
clmax falls and minimum cd rises

explanation: Higher Re gives a thinner boundary layer with more momentum near the wall, delaying separation (higher clmax). The skin-friction coefficient falls roughly as Re^(−0.2) turbulent or Re^(−0.5) laminar.

question: At low Reynolds number (below ~5 × 10⁵), a section's boundary layer typically:

options.text: Separates laminar and may reattach turbulent, forming a laminar separation bubble
Remains fully laminar to the trailing edge at all α
Becomes turbulent immediately at the leading edge

explanation: A laminar layer cannot sustain the adverse gradient behind the suction peak; it separates, transitions in the free shear layer, and may reattach. The bubble raises drag and can burst at higher α, causing an abrupt stall.

question: On a tapered wing the tip chord Reynolds number is 0.4 of the root value. The effect on stall progression is:

options.text: Higher local clmax at the tip, delaying tip stall
No effect, because Re affects only drag
Root stall, because the root Re is higher
Lower local clmax at the tip, aggravating tip-stall tendency

explanation: Re ∝ chord. Lower Re lowers the section clmax. Combined with the higher local cl demanded outboard on a tapered wing, the tip reaches its limit first.

question: A laminar-flow section operates at a cl outside its low-drag bucket. The profile drag:

options.text: Falls, since the section is off-design
Rises sharply, as transition moves forward on one surface

explanation: The bucket exists only where the favourable gradient holds on both surfaces. Above the bucket the suction peak forms near the upper leading edge; below it, near the lower. Transition then moves forward on that surface and skin friction jumps.

question: A section achieves L/D = 100 at cl = 0.8 (cd = 0.008). A wing using it has A = 8 and e = 0.85 at CL = 0.8. Ignoring other drag, the wing's L/D is closest to:
explanation: CD,i = 0.64/(π × 0.85 × 8) = 0.64/21.36 = 0.030. CD = 0.008 + 0.030 = 0.038 → L/D = 0.8/0.038 = 21. Induced drag, not section drag, dominates finite-wing efficiency at this CL.
